sections.title: Decisions we need from you
sections.lede: Six items. Each has a default so you are confirming, not authoring. Reply with the number and yes, or the number and what you want changed.

items.q: The tip credit campaign now runs on the corrected premise.
items.context: The original hook was that a net loss disqualifies a restaurant from the FICA tip credit and that Paychex claims it on the client's behalf through its EIN. We verified both halves against primary sources and neither holds. The section 45B credit is a general business credit under section 38: nonrefundable, but section 39 carries it back one year and forward twenty. And 26 CFR 31.3511-1 assigns section 45B, section 51, section 1396 and section 45S to the CPEO's customer, not the CPEO. The corrected angle is stronger: the credit was always the client's, most operators have never filed Form 8846, and as of tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 it reaches barbering, hair care, nail care, esthetics, and body and spa treatment.
items.default: Run on the corrected premise. Retire the EIN framing everywhere.

items.q: Fred reports a weekly referral count in two buckets.
items.context: The A/B test compares traffic sent straight to the Paychex referral form against traffic sent to our landing page. Because the two arms have different destinations, the pipe a lead arrives through is the arm. Fred counts leads that came via the referral form separately from leads that came via our handoff. We need a fixed day, a named recipient, a written definition of what counts as a referral, and a four-week baseline before launch.
items.default: Fridays, to Robert and Johnathon, with a referral defined as a name plus a scheduled conversation.

items.q: The Offerings Lockup is cleared for an insurance agency partner.
items.context: The Paychex guidelines say not to use the HR | Payroll | Benefits | Insurance lockup where it creates channel conflict, and name Bank and Financial Advisors as examples. Protect Health is an insurance agency. The Winning Team flyer, dated March 2026, uses the full lockup with the Protect Health mark, so precedent says we are clear. We would rather confirm than assume.
items.default: Use the lockup as the Winning Team flyer does.

items.q: Document control numbers for partner-produced PEO pieces.
items.context: Every Paychex PEO piece carries a control number and date in its legal footer, such as 173193 03/10/2026 on the Winning Team flyer. We cannot invent one. Tonight's creative avoids the problem by keeping PEO language off net-new assets and reserving it for the landing page, which mirrors your approved layout.
items.default: Reuse 173193 on anything that is a direct derivative of the Winning Team flyer. Keep PEO claims off other creative until you tell us the process.

items.q: Email to the Protect Health list goes to employer contacts only.
items.context: The list is largely individual health insurance clients. Sending a payroll and HR offer to individuals who bought an ACA plan is an audience mismatch that costs deliverability, and the domain already has open bounce and suppression work. We segment to business owners and employer contacts, and use the portal's second template with Fred in the rep slot.
items.default: Employer contacts only. Individual clients receive nothing from this campaign.

items.q: Launch sequencing: TOFU first, ladder two weeks later.
items.context: The 25/50/75 view-depth audiences only exist for video and need time to fill before the retargeting layer has anyone in it. Even on a clean approval, top of funnel launches first and the retargeting ladder switches on once the buckets have volume.
items.default: Approve the sequence as drawn in the timeline.

sections.title: One story, five doors
sections.lede: Every asset in this plan makes the same argument. A Nevada employer's payroll is a tax asset they are not claiming, and the reason they are not claiming it is structure, not eligibility.

blocks.text: That sentence does a lot of work. It is true for a restaurant that never filed Form 8846. It is true for a contractor who assumed a 401(k) was out of reach and never ran the section 45E credit math. It is true for a salon owner who has spent thirty years being told, correctly at the time, that the tip credit was a restaurant thing. And it points at Paychex as the mechanism without requiring us to make a single claim about tax outcomes.

Under the umbrella sit five doors. Each is a reason an employer might walk in. They share creative, they share the landing page, and they share the retargeting ladder. What differs is the first sentence.

blocks.title: Why the hiring door was retired
blocks.text: The work opportunity tax credit lapsed after December 31, 2025 and has not been extended. Department of Labor guidance in TEGL No. 09-25, dated April 28, 2026, states that state workforce agencies may not issue certifications during a lapse. Nevada's own DETR pages still present the program as active, which is why employers here keep hearing it is live. The only honest residual step is filing Form 8850 within 28 days of hire to preserve position in case Congress extends retroactively. That is one Q&A page, not a campaign.

sections.title: Why three stages, and why in this order
sections.lede: You know what a funnel is. What follows is why this specific shape, because the shape is doing work that a single landing page and a single ad cannot.

blocks.text: Top of funnel earns attention from people who do not know they have a problem

A salon owner is not searching for the FICA tip credit. They do not know it applies to them. A contractor is not searching for the section 45E startup credit. They assumed a 401(k) cost too much and stopped thinking about it. These people cannot be reached with an offer, because an offer answers a question they have not asked.

So the top of funnel makes no offer. It states a fact the viewer believes is wrong, and stops. No button, no form, no call to action. Its only job is to sort the audience. People who watch to the end have told us something about themselves without filling out anything. That signal is the raw material for everything below it.
Middle of funnel is where someone who now believes the problem is real compares their options

Once an owner accepts that the state retirement program is not a benefit they offer, the next question is what the alternatives cost. Once a restaurant owner accepts that a loss year did not destroy the credit, the next question is who computes it. These are comparison questions, and they get comparison content: the state program head to head with a 401(k), the PEO as a credit-capture mechanism rather than a buying decision.

Middle of funnel content points somewhere. A calculator, an article, a longer video. It still does not ask for contact information, because asking early is what kills small-employer funnels. The owner is evaluating, and an opt-in form at this stage reads as a sales trap.
Bottom of funnel is where the opt-in lives, once and only once

The landing page carries the single ask. By the time someone arrives, they have seen the fact, considered the comparison, and chosen to look at what we do about it. The page's job is to make the next step feel like the obvious continuation of what they were already doing, which is why it leads with a mechanism and a proof, then asks, then offers the reading library below the form for anyone who wants more before committing.
The same shape runs twice

Organic and paid follow the same three stages. The blog clusters are the organic version: three top-of-funnel articles feeding two middle-of-funnel articles feeding one bottom-of-funnel page, each article carrying four question-and-answer children, twenty-five URLs per cluster, structured to be cited by Google's AI answers and by ChatGPT. The paid version is the retargeting ladder described below. They point at the same landing page. That is what makes it one system rather than two campaigns.

blocks.title: The employer-tax cluster is the proof this shape exists
blocks.text: Sixteen pages are built and committed: three top-of-funnel posts on the Nevada retirement mandate, small business retirement plan tax credits, and Section 125 payroll tax savings, with twelve question-and-answer children and the bottom-of-funnel hub. Ten more pages are written for the middle: the state program against a 401(k), the PEO as a credit mechanism, and eight children including two correction pages. Two of the sixteen are correction pages, one on the WOTC lapse and one on the absence of any published Nevada non-compliance penalty. Nobody else in the market is answering either correctly, and when an AI model has conflicting inputs, the source that names and corrects the common error is the one it cites.

sections.title: Who we reach, and on which platform
sections.lede: LinkedIn and Meta are not doing the same job. Treating them the same is the fastest way to burn budget.

blocks.text: LinkedIn is the only platform where we can target by company size, industry and job title. That makes it the right place for cold reach against a tight firmographic filter: owner or general manager titles at companies with six to one hundred employees in Clark County, in the industries each door speaks to. It is expensive per impression and it should be used for exactly one thing, which is finding people we cannot otherwise identify.

Meta is where the retargeting economics work. Video view audiences, engagement audiences, landing page visitors, all of it is cheaper and more precise on Meta than anywhere else. The 25/50/75 ladder lives here. So does the volume top-of-funnel that fills it.

blocks.title: Keep the two tip audiences separate
blocks.text: The beauty-services video and the loss-year video both sit on the tip credit, but they target different people. Running both to the same audience makes them compete in the same auction and doubles the cost of reaching either. Restaurants get the loss-year piece. Beauty services get the expansion piece.

sections.title: The path from ad to broker
sections.lede: What happens after someone clicks matters more to Paychex than the creative does. Here is every hop.

blocks.text: The click lands on our landing page with UTMs identifying the platform, the door, and the creative. The page loads our tracking first, then renders. The form posts to our CRM with formId set to employers, which routes it to the employer pipeline, and the Landing Page field records the URL, which is what separates these leads from everything else in the system.

Inside the CRM the lead is assigned and a broker is notified. The broker makes the first call. Benefits conversations stay with us. Payroll and HR conversations are handed to Fred with the PartnerId intact, so Paychex's own attribution sees Protect Health as the source. Fred reports back weekly in two buckets, which is how the A/B test gets its primary number.
The split CTA

The landing page carries two calls to action. One captures to our form. The other links to the Paychex referral form with PartnerId=461541 attached, for the visitor who already knows they want payroll and does not want to talk to a broker first. Our tracking event fires before that redirect so we see the click even though we never see the submission.

blocks.title: Tracking is verified before any ad runs
blocks.text: PartnerId=461541 has to survive every hop. Redirects, link shorteners and QR generators all strip query parameters, so every outbound link is tested after every page edit. Meta pixel and Conversions API confirmed. LinkedIn Insight Tag installed. UTM taxonomy written down before the first campaign is built, not reverse-engineered from the first report.

sections.title: The retargeting ladder
sections.lede: Video viewers sort themselves by how long they watch. We speak to each bucket differently, because how long someone watched tells us what they already believe.

blocks.text: Every top-of-funnel video is twenty-five to thirty seconds and carries no call to action. Meta records how much of it each viewer watched. We build three audiences from that: people who watched at least a quarter, people who watched at least half, and people who watched at least three quarters. Each bucket gets its own follow-up creative, and the copy changes with the depth.

head: Bucket
What we know about them
What they see next
Copy posture
rows: The hook held them, then they left. They saw the claim, not the reasoning.
A different top-of-funnel video on the same door, or a static restating the fact with one supporting number.

Compare. Point somewhere. Still no form.
They watched nearly all of it. The reasoning landed.

blocks.text: The ladder only works if the buckets have volume, which is why the timeline launches top of funnel first and switches on the retargeting layer roughly two weeks later. Launching everything on the same day means the retargeting ads run to empty audiences and the platform reads that as a failure.
Frequency and exit

Each bucket sees its follow-up no more than three times over ten days. Anyone who reaches the landing page exits the ladder regardless of bucket. Anyone who submits the form is suppressed from all campaign audiences the same day, so we never show an ad to someone the broker is already calling.

sections.title: Organic first, then paid behind the winners
sections.lede: Organic posts are the cheapest test we have. The ones that earn attention on their own are the ones that get budget.

blocks.text: Every video and static runs organically on the Protect Health pages before it runs as an ad. That gives us a read on which door and which framing the audience responds to, at zero media cost. Then we put money behind the winners and leave the rest alone.
The promotion trigger, defined so it is not an argument

A post earns paid budget when, over its first seven days, it clears two thresholds against the account's trailing thirty-day median: at least double the median saves and shares, and at least one and a half times the median average watch time for video or engagement rate for static. Both, not either. Saves and shares indicate the content was worth keeping. Watch time indicates the reasoning held. A post that spikes on one and not the other is usually a hook that did not pay off.

The boost budget is fixed per winning post and runs for fourteen days to the cold audience for that door. Winners that also perform under paid spend become the permanent creative for that door's top of funnel. Everything else rotates out.

sections.title: The three top-of-funnel videos
sections.lede: All three are corrections, because a correction is the only pattern interrupt that survives contact with a skeptical business owner. The first line has to work as on-screen text, because most of the audience sees it with sound off.

blocks.title: V1: The Nevada retirement mandate
blocks.why: Every owner running the state program thinks they are offering a retirement benefit. They are running a payroll deduction they are legally barred from contributing to.
lines: Nevada won't fine you for ignoring the retirement mandate. There's no penalty published. That's not the reason to pay attention.
The reason is what the state program actually is. It's a Roth IRA the employee owns. You facilitate the deduction. You are not permitted to put a single dollar in.
So when you tell a candidate you offer retirement, and the shop down the street says they match four percent, those are not two versions of the same thing.
Seventy-five hundred a year in the state program. Twenty-four thousand five hundred in a 401k, before your match.
blocks.onscreen: The two numbers, side by side, held for the last four seconds.
blocks.sources: IRS Notice 2025-67 for the contribution limits. NRS 353D for the absence of a penalty provision. Nevada Treasurer program materials for the employer-contribution prohibition.

blocks.title: V2: The 2025 tip credit expansion
blocks.why: Thousands of Clark County salon, barbershop, nail and spa owners have spent their careers being told correctly that the tip credit was a restaurant thing. It stopped being true in 2025 and nobody told them.
lines: If your business takes tips and you are not a restaurant, a federal tax credit opened up to you last year and almost nobody has mentioned it.
The FICA tip credit used to cover food and beverage only. For tax years starting after December 2024 it now reaches barbering and hair care, nail care, esthetics, and body and spa treatment.
Same credit restaurants have claimed for thirty years. One page, Form 8846.
Most salon owners in this valley have never filed it once. Not because they don't qualify. Because nobody told them they do.
blocks.onscreen: The four service categories listed, one per line, as they are named.
blocks.sources: IRC section 45B as amended by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Form 8846 instructions.

blocks.title: V3: The loss year correction
blocks.why: It contradicts something their own accountant told them, which is the strongest interrupt available, and it is verifiable in the code.
lines: Your accountant told you a loss year means you can't use the tip credit. That's half right, and the half they left out is worth real money.
The credit is nonrefundable. True. It can't generate a refund. Also true.
But it carries back one year and forward twenty. A loss doesn't destroy the credit. It parks it until you're profitable again.
Which means the businesses losing this money aren't the ones with losses. They're the ones who heard disqualified and never filed the form.
blocks.onscreen: The words carries forward 20 years, held long.
blocks.sources: IRC section 38 for nonrefundability. IRC section 39 for the one-year carryback and twenty-year carryforward. Form 8846 and Form 3800 instructions.

blocks.title: Production notes
blocks.text: Twenty-five to thirty seconds each, slow and observational, no fast cuts, no music bed pushing urgency. Bright, white-dominant, real Southern Nevada workplaces. Nothing in these three triggers Lane C: no dollar math of our own, no Nevada penalty figure, no live WOTC claim, no advice on what anyone should do. Paychex is not named in the top-of-funnel videos and the Paychex mark does not appear, which keeps them entirely in Protect Health's voice and out of the brand review queue.

blocks.title: Why organic is a full week ahead of paid
blocks.text: The seven-day organic read is what decides which creative gets budget. Launching paid on the same day as organic means spending on a guess. One week of lag is the cost of spending on evidence.

sections.title: Compliance
sections.lede: Three lanes, and the lines we do not cross regardless of lane.

head: Lane
What it covers
What it needs
rows: Paychex published language used verbatim: portal copy blocks, approved stats with attribution, the video introductions, the testimonial.
Our copy built on Paychex published figures. Nevada law and IRS rules stated with primary-source citations.
Our own math, our own claims about outcomes, anything an employer could read as tax advice.
Sean's written approval and a source log. We are avoiding Lane C in this wave entirely.

blocks.text: Claims we do not make anywhere
No Nevada non-compliance penalty figure, in any form, including hedged. Nevada publishes none. The figures in circulation belong to California, Illinois and Colorado.
No claim that WOTC is currently claimable. It lapsed after December 31, 2025 and state agencies cannot certify during a lapse.
No claim that a PEO claims tax credits on a client's behalf, or that a net loss disqualifies a business from the tip credit. Both are wrong and both were in the original brief. See decision one.

No dollar figures of our own. Every number is either an IRS limit, a statutory provision, or a Paychex published statistic used verbatim with attribution. Where a page needs an estimate, it points at Paychex's own calculators.
No tax advice. Every page carries the line that we are insurance nerds, not tax professionals, and recommends a CPA before acting.
Brand rules on every co-branded asset

Paychex Blue is #0059a2 exactly. The mark appears only on white or near-white, never on tan, never on a photograph, never on a low-contrast field, with one cap-height of clear space on all sides. We use the Offerings Lockup in the three sizes supplied and do not recolor, trace, angle, or otherwise alter it. Where a dark surface needs Paychex attribution, the name appears in type, not the mark. Co-branded footers follow the Winning Team flyer: Protect Health left, Paychex right, on white. Every PEO piece carries the Paychex Business Solutions and Oasis Outsourcing legal block, the copyright line, and a document control number.
